q-184672.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- If an integer $n$ is even, then there exists an integer $p$ such that $n=2p.$

- If an integer $n$ is odd, then there exists an integer $q$ such that $n=2q+1.$

In this case, we need to prove the following:

$$
{n}^{3}-1\text{ is even}\,⇒\,n\text{ is odd}
$$

To prove $P⇒Q,$ it suffices to prove the contrapositive $¬Q⇒¬P.$

The contrapositive form of the given statement is

$$
n\text{ is not odd}\,⇒\,{n}^{3}-1\text{ is not even}
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
n\text{ is even}\,⇒\,{n}^{3}-1\text{ is odd}.
$$

We start by using the fact that $n$ is even.

If $n$ is $\text{even},$ then
$n=2a,$
where $a$ is $\text{an integer}.$

The idea is to substitute $n=2a$ into the expression ${n}^{3}-1$ and show it is odd by writing it as  one more than a multiple of $2.$

Substituting $n=2a$ into the expression ${n}^{3}-1,$ we can show that ${n}^{3}-1=2b+1,$ where $b$ is $\text{an integer}.$

Once we've done this, the proof is complete, and we can state our conclusion.

Therefore, since ${n}^{3}-1$ $\text{is one more than}$ a multiple of $2,$ we conclude that ${n}^{3}-1$ is $\text{odd}.$

$$
n\text{ is not even}\,⇒\,5n+4\text{ is not even}
